sentences.text: The bush moa is the sole species within the genus Anomalopteryx and is an extinct bird found only in New Zealand.
Adults of this species are estimated to have weighed between 30 and 49 kilograms.
Like other moa, it possessed a sternum but lacked a keel.
Its sturdy, sharp-edged beak was adapted for eating twigs and tough plant material.
Bush moa eggs measured 15.2 to 18 cm in length and 11.5 to 12.1 cm in width, making them larger than ostrich eggs.
Richard Owen first scientifically described the bush moa in 1844 under the name Dinornis didiformis.
Coprolites indicate that ferns were a crucial food source for the bush moa.
Scientists have assembled a nearly complete genome of the bush moa from toe bones, suggesting it could potentially be resurrected using the emu as a proxy.
The bush moa has been classified under several synonyms including Dinornis didiformis, Dinornis parvus, and Anomalopteryx antiquus.
The bush moa inhabited much of New Zealand's North Island and some sections of the South Island.
The genus Anomalopteryx existed from the Gelasian to the Holocene, spanning from 2.58 to 0 million years ago.
